extracted.intended_audience: poets, literary critics, and students of poetry
extracted.subtask_description: Didactic guidance on how to write poetry well and how critics should judge poetry — covering taste, judgment, style, moral conduct, and technical craft. The page lays out principles for both producing verse and evaluating it fairly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Critics should have written well
rubrics_metrics.description: Let such teach others who themselves excel, And censure freely, who have written well.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A legitimate critic is one who has practical accomplishment — those who 'have written well' may 'censure freely'. Implicit anti-pattern: critics who have not practiced the art lack authority.

rubrics_metrics.name: Know your own reach; stay within your depth
rubrics_metrics.description: Be sure yourself and your own reach to know / How far your genius taste and learning go. Launch not beyond your depth, but be discreet / And mark that point where sense and dullness meet.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Critics (and writers) must be honest about their limits and refrain from judging areas beyond their competence. Avoid overreaching ambition and the mistake of pretending greater knowledge than you have.

rubrics_metrics.name: Follow nature as the primary norm
rubrics_metrics.description: First follow nature and your judgment frame / By her just standard, which is still the same.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat 'nature' (truth, life, common human perception) as the test of art: art should serve life and natural expression. 'Nature' is described as an unerring, universal light and the source/end/test of art.

rubrics_metrics.name: Learn from the ancients; rules are 'nature methodized'
rubrics_metrics.description: Those rules, of old discovered, not devised, / Are nature still, but nature methodized.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Study classical exemplars (Homer, Horace, Greek models) to derive precepts. Use ancient rules as distilled nature; be guided by classical examples rather than fashion alone.

rubrics_metrics.name: Justified license is permissible but rare
rubrics_metrics.description: If, where the rules not far enough extend ... Some lucky license answer to the full / The intent proposed that license is a rule.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Great writers may 'gloriously offend' and take liberties when necessity and precedent justify them; deviations should be exceptional, purposeful, and defensible by precedent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid being 'half-learned' or 'bookful blockhead' — value true understanding
rubrics_metrics.description: Those half-learned witlings ... Unfinished things one knows not what to call ... The bookful blockhead ignorantly read, / With loads of learned lumber in his head.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Superficial erudition that substitutes memorized learning for real judgment is a flaw. Avoid parroting authorities; prefer internalized understanding and sense.

rubrics_metrics.name: A little learning is dangerous — study deeply
rubrics_metrics.description: A little learning is a dangerous thing / Drink deep, or taste not the Pierian spring.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Surface acquaintance with knowledge intoxicates; those who only 'taste' the field make worse critics. Thorough study sobers judgment; shallow study leads to error and conceit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Judge a work in the spirit of its author
rubrics_metrics.description: A perfect judge will read each work of wit / With the same spirit that its author writ.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess a piece according to its aims and the tone the author intended. Avoid applying inappropriate standards or seeking faults that are inconsistent with the author's purpose.

rubrics_metrics.name: Regard the writer's end; judge by purpose and means
rubrics_metrics.description: In every work regard the writer's end, / Since none can compass more than they intend; / And if the means be just, the conduct true, / Applause, in spite of trivial faults, is due.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider the intended effect and scope of a work; if means are appropriate to ends, minor faults should not negate merit. This is an instruction to weight intention and execution rather than perfectionism.

rubrics_metrics.name: True wit is nature to advantage dressed
rubrics_metrics.description: True wit is nature to advantage dressed; / What oft was thought, but ne'er so well expressed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Genuine cleverness or poetic insight refines and expresses nature, rather than merely dazzling with novelty. Avoid baroque ornament that masks weak thought.

rubrics_metrics.name: Match style to subject; avoid false eloquence
rubrics_metrics.description: Expression is the dress of thought, and still / Appears more decent, as more suitable; / A vile conceit in pompous words expressed, / Is like a clown in regal purple dressed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose diction and rhetorical devices appropriate to the subject. 'False eloquence' — gaudy style without substance — is condemned. Style should illuminate thought, not overshadow it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Different subjects require different styles
rubrics_metrics.description: For different styles with different subjects sort, / As several garbs with country town and court.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adapt tone, diction, and form to the content and context. Ancients vs. moderns, plain vs. ornate — use the style that fits subject and audience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid extremes in judgment and taste
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid extremes, and shun the fault of such, / Who still are pleased too little or too much.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Moderation is a virtue: neither universal praise nor universal scorn is wise. Beware of critics who are always offended or always impressed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sound should echo sense — musicality must fit meaning
rubrics_metrics.description: True ease in writing comes from art, not chance ... 'Tis not enough no harshness gives offense, / The sound must seem an echo to the sense.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prosody and sonic qualities (rhythm, cadence, meter) should reinforce meaning: loud, rough verse for force; smooth numbers for softer scenes. Musical variation must serve the content.

rubrics_metrics.name: Vary rhythm to fit changing passions
rubrics_metrics.description: Hear how Timotheus' varied lays surprise, / And bid alternate passions fall and rise!
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Employ shifts in rhythm and cadence to produce emotional movement in verse. Imitate the musical examples of ancient practice — alternation of passion and repose.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid mechanical, monotonous devices (expletives, forced rhymes, pointless Alexandrines)
rubrics_metrics.description: These equal syllables alone require ... While expletives their feeble aid do join; / And ten low words oft creep in one dull line, ... And, at the last and only couplet fraught / With some unmeaning thing they call a thought, / A needless Alexandrine ends the song.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Anti-patterns of mediocre poetry include slavish syllabic regularity, piling up expletives, tired images that recur line-to-line, and tacked-on terminal Alexandrines. Prefer natural ease and meaningful closure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not judge by an author's name; judge the work
rubrics_metrics.description: Some judge of authors names not works, and then / Nor praise nor blame the writing, but the men.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid reputational bias: praise or blame should be based on the writing itself, not the social status or reputation of the author.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid following the crowd; form judgments independently
rubrics_metrics.description: Some ne'er advance a judgment of their own, / But catch the spreading notion of the town, / They reason and conclude by precedent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Resist bandwagon thinking and critical conformity. Seek independent appraisal rather than relying on prevailing public opinion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Support genuine merit early; do not wait for consensus
rubrics_metrics.description: Be thou the first true merit to befriend / His praise is lost who stays till all commend.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Encourage deserving writers promptly rather than deferring praise until popularity establishes merit. Early critical support can help merit survive envy and neglect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not excuse obscenity even when clever
rubrics_metrics.description: No pardon vile obscenity should find, / Though wit and art conspire to move your mind;
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Moral limits: avoid forgiving obscenity or base subject matter just because of craft or wit. Critics should condemn obscenity irrespective of technical skill.

rubrics_metrics.name: Combine truth and candor with good breeding in criticism
rubrics_metrics.description: In all you speak, let truth and candor shine ... Without good breeding truth is disapproved; / That only makes superior sense beloved.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Deliver honest criticism with tact and civility. The manner of speech matters: blunt truths can harm; polite, well-bred discourse makes reasoned sense persuasive and welcomed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be silent when unsure; speak with diffidence when certain
rubrics_metrics.description: Be silent always, when you doubt your sense; / And speak, though sure, with seeming diffidence:
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exercise modesty: refrain from pronouncing when uncertain, and temper even confident judgments with modest phrasing to avoid arrogance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Teach gently — instruct as if you taught not
rubrics_metrics.description: Men must be taught as if you taught them not, / And things unknown proposed as things forgot.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Critical pedagogy should be subtle: present instructive remarks as gentle suggestions rather than pedantic lessons; help readers/writers discover rather than feel lectured.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be generous with advice; avoid 'avarice of sense'
rubrics_metrics.description: Be niggards of advice on no pretense; / For the worst avarice is that of sense.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not withhold useful guidance. Critics should share insights and corrections freely rather than hoarding judgment as a display of superiority.

rubrics_metrics.name: Restrain censure when it does no good; sometimes silence is best
rubrics_metrics.description: Tis best sometimes your censure to restrain, / And charitably let the dull be vain / Your silence there is better than your spite, / For who can rail so long as they can write?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Repeated attacks on bad writers may be futile; letting incompetent writers continue may be wiser than deriding them endlessly. Use restraint to avoid amplifying folly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ideal critic: unbiased, learned, humane, modestly bold, and generous
rubrics_metrics.description: Unbiased, or by favor, or in spite, / Not dully prepossessed, nor blindly right; / Though learned, well-bred, and though well bred, sincere, / Modestly bold, and humanly severe, / Who to a friend his faults can freely show, / And gladly praise the merit of a foe?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A critic should be impartial (not swayed by favor or spite), well-informed, courteous, sincere, willing to rebuke friends and praise enemies, and combine firmness with humanity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Historical awareness: understand authors' contexts and ages
rubrics_metrics.description: Know well each ancient's proper character, / His fable subject scope in every page, / Religion, country, genius of his age.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Contextual knowledge of an author's era, national character, beliefs and typical subjects is necessary to judge their work properly; do not apply anachronistic standards without accounting for context.

rubrics_metrics.name: Repress license with useful laws; uphold rules that promote art
rubrics_metrics.description: Thus long succeeding critics justly reigned, / License repressed, and useful laws ordained.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Critical norms and rules exist to curb excess and preserve standards; critics should enforce constructive boundaries while recognizing where rules serve art's ends.
